query: When is the next leap year?

results.title: When Is the Next Leap Year? 2028 | Date & the Rule
results.content:
Quick Reference: The Next Leap Year
Next leap day: Tuesday, February 29, 2028
The rule: Divisible by 4, except century years not divisible by 400
Next non-leap century year: 2100
Calendar in use: Gregorian (in place since 1582)
The next leap year is 2028, and leap day falls on Tuesday, February 29, 2028. The rule is simple in one breath and tricky in the fine print: a year is a leap year if it divides evenly by 4, with one exception for century years. Below is the date you need, the next five leap years on the calendar, the full Gregorian rule explained in plain English, and the long history of why we add a day to February in the first place.
When Is the Next Leap Year?
The next leap year is 2028. February 29, 2028 falls on a Tuesday. After that, the leap years arrive every four years on a steady cadence: 2032, 2036, 2040, 2044, and on through the rest of the century. The only break in that four-year rhythm comes at century years; the next one of those that skips a leap day is 2100.
The last leap year was 2024, so we are currently two years into a non-leap stretch. February 2026 has 28 days; February 2027 will also have 28 days; February 2028 will have 29.
Year — Leap Day
2028 — Tuesday, February 29
2032 — Sunday, February 29
2036 — Friday, February 29
2040 — Wednesday, February 29
2044 — Monday, February 29
The weekday on which leap day lands shifts by five each cycle. That is because four common years move the day of the week forward by four, and the leap day itself bumps it one more. Mark the date that lines up with the kind of weekend you want: 2032 puts February 29 on a Sunday, 2036 lands it on a Friday, and 2044 turns it into a long Monday.
Full Moon Dates, To-the-Minute
Leap day in 2028 falls a week after the Full Snow Moon. See every 2026 full Moon, with exact timestamps and the traditional name for each.
The reason for the extra day comes down to a mismatch between two clocks: the tidy 365-day calendar on the wall and the actual time the Earth takes to orbit the Sun. A trip around the Sun (a tropical year or solar year) does not land neatly on 365 days. It runs 365.242199 days, which is 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes, and 46 seconds, according to NASA.
Those leftover hours pile up. Six hours a year becomes a full day every four years. If we ignored them, the calendar would drift away from the seasons; after a few centuries, February would be a summer month and June would be deep winter in the Northern Hemisphere. The leap day is the patch that keeps the spring equinox on or about March 20 and the harvest moon in autumn where it belongs.
Why Do We Call It a “Leap” Year?
A common (non-leap) year is exactly 52 weeks plus one day. That extra day is the reason a birthday that lands on a Tuesday in one common year lands on a Wednesday the next. A leap year, by contrast, is 52 weeks plus two days. If your birthday fell on a Wednesday last year, in a leap year it “leaps” past Thursday and lands on Friday. That weekday jump is where the name “leap year” comes from.
The Rule: Divisible by 4, Except
The Gregorian rule for leap years is three lines long:
A year is a leap year if it is evenly divisible by 4.
Century years (those ending in 00) are not leap years.
Except a century year is a leap year if it is evenly divisible by 400.
The exception inside the exception is the part that trips people up. In practice it means a small handful of century years that look like leap years on the four-rule are not. The years 1700, 1800, and 1900 were not leap years; they divide by 4 but they also divide by 100 without dividing by 400. The year 2000 was a leap year; it divides by 400, so the second exception turned it back into a leap year. The next century year to skip leap day is 2100, then 2200, then 2300. The next one to keep it is 2400.
That double exception is not a quirk; it is what makes the calendar accurate. The plain four-year rule overshoots by about 11 minutes a year, so the century-year correction trims about three days every 400 years. The math works out to an average year length of 365.2425 days, which is within roughly 26 seconds of the true solar year.
Leap day is an artifact that dates back to 46 BC, when Julius Caesar took the advice of the learned astronomer Sosigenes of Alexandria. Sosigenes knew from Egyptian experience that the Earth takes 365.25 days to circle the Sun. To absorb that residual quarter day, an extra day was added to the calendar every four years. The new “Julian” calendar was used throughout the Roman Empire and by various Christian churches. At that time, February was the last month of the year.
To make a proper transition from the old Roman calendar (which had 355 days and was basically a lunar calendar) to the Julian calendar, and to get the months and various feasts and holidays back into their normal seasons, ninety extra days were inserted into the year 46 BC. Caesar divided the ninety extra days into three temporary months.
One month was added between February and March. Two others, Intercalaris Prior and Intercalaris Posterior, were added after November. (That phrasing explains why leap years are still sometimes called intercalary years.) The end result was a single year that ran fifteen months and 445 days long. The Romans nicknamed it Annus Confusionus, the “Year of Confusion.”
Later, to honor his contribution to timekeeping, Caesar renamed the fifth month (formerly known as Quintilis) after himself. That is the July on every calendar today.
The Julian calendar worked so well at first that many countries adopted it. It was, however, slightly flawed. The Julian year ran .0078 of a day (about 11 minutes and 14 seconds) longer than the tropical year. That tiny excess introduced an error of one day every 128 years. Every 128 years, the tropical year shifted one day backward against the calendar. The drift made the method for calculating the date of Easter steadily less accurate.
By the year 1582, thanks to centuries of observing one leap year too many, the calendar had fallen out of step with the solar year by a full 10 days. It was then that Pope Gregory XIII stepped in. With the advice of a German Jesuit mathematician and astronomer, Christopher Clavius, he produced the calendar we still use, the Gregorian calendar.
Building a Better Calendar
First, to catch things up, ten days were omitted after Thursday, October 4, 1582. The next day on the new calendar was Friday, October 15. For many people the edict was wildly unpopular; it was as if ten days had been taken from their lives. There were riots in the streets, and workers demanded their ten days of pay (forgetting, conveniently, that they had not worked those ten days). Eventually, all the calendrical flak died down.
Next, to more closely match the length of the tropical year, century years that would have been leap years on the old Julian rule were quietly dropped. The exceptions, as before, were the century years equally divisible by 400, not just by 4. That single tweak is the reason the year 2000 was a leap year and 1700, 1800, and 1900 were not.
The Gregorian calendar was not adopted everywhere at once. Catholic countries switched in 1582. Protestant ones held out for decades. The American Colonies, then under British rule, did not adopt the new calendar until 1752. The British Empire skipped the days September 3 through September 13, 1752; the day after Wednesday, September 2, 1752 was Thursday, September 14. That eleven-day jump is the reason George Washington was, in a real sense, not born on Washington’s Birthday.
In our time we celebrate Washington’s Birthday on February 22. That is correct on the Gregorian calendar, but George was born twenty years before the Colonies switched. When he was born, the error in the Julian calendar had grown to eleven days. The calendar hanging on the wall in the Washington household that morning would have read February 11, 1732.
If the twenty years it took the American Colonies to ratify the Gregorian reform sounds long, it is nothing compared to Russia, which finally accepted calendar reformation in 1918. Greece held out even longer, all the way to 1923.
Leap Day Traditions and Folklore
Leap day has collected a thick crust of folklore over the centuries. Most of the traditions point in the same direction: leap day is the day the ordinary rules of the calendar pause, so the ordinary rules of social life pause along with them.
Bachelor’s Day in Ireland. The oldest leap-day tradition holds that on February 29, a woman could propose marriage to a man without breaking custom. Irish legend traces the practice to a 5th-century deal between Saint Brigid of Kildare and Saint Patrick, with Patrick agreeing the proposal could be made once every leap year.
Sadie Hawkins. The American spin on the same idea is Sadie Hawkins Day, named for a character in Al Capp’s Li’l Abner comic strip in the 1930s. It is not strictly tied to leap day, but the pairing has stuck in popular memory.
Scotland’s 1288 statute. Folk history holds that Queen Margaret of Scotland passed a 1288 law allowing women to propose on leap day, with a fine in silk or gloves for any man who refused. Historians are skeptical that the statute ever existed, but the story has had remarkable staying power.
Leaplings. People born on February 29 are called “leaplings” or “leapers.” There are roughly five million of them worldwide. Most celebrate their birthday on February 28 or March 1 in common years; legally, most jurisdictions treat March 1 as the next-day equivalent.
The unlucky-marriage strand. In Greece, marrying in a leap year is considered bad luck, and marrying on leap day specifically is considered worse. Roughly one in five engaged couples in Greece will reschedule to avoid a leap-year wedding.
The odds of being born on February 29 are roughly 1 in 1,461. A handful of famous leaplings have made the most of the rarity:
Ja Rule (rapper and actor), born February 29, 1976.
Tony Robbins (motivational speaker and author), born February 29, 1960.
Dinah Shore (singer and television host), born February 29, 1916.
Antonio Sabato Jr. (actor), born February 29, 1972.
Pope Paul III, born February 29, 1468.
Many leaplings keep their official paperwork age in years they have lived, not in birthdays they have had. A leapling born in 2000 has lived 26 years as of 2026 but has technically had only six “real” birthdays.
Leap Year Superstitions Around the World
Beyond the proposal traditions, leap years carry their own grab bag of superstitions. We pair them with our usual measured caveat: folk traditions are worth knowing because they are part of the calendar’s culture, not because we vouch for the predictions.
Greece: Leap-year marriages bring bad luck; leap-day marriages, worse.
Scotland: A 1288 statute (real or folk) said women could propose on leap day, and a man who refused paid a fine.
Italy: The proverb anno bisesto, anno funesto, “leap year, gloomy year,” holds that leap years bring bad weather and bad fortune. Major life decisions, especially weddings, are sometimes pushed to a non-leap year.
Russia (folk): Leap years bring more freak weather and more deaths in the family, according to peasant tradition.
Taiwan: Married daughters traditionally return home during the leap month of the lunisolar calendar to bring their parents pig-trotter noodles, said to ward off bad luck in the parents’ year.
Should We Do Away With Leap Years?
The Gregorian calendar has proven far more accurate than the Julian. Over the span of a single year it runs only about 26 seconds too fast. The error is so small that it would not be necessary to drop a day from the calendar until somewhere around the year 5300.
Even so, some calendar reformers would like to see ours redrawn. One of the more popular proposals is the World Calendar, created by Elisabeth Achelis of The World Calendar Association in 1930. It consists of 364 days. The year would be divided into four equal quarters, each quarter consisting of three months. The first month of each new quarter (January, April, July, October) would have 31 days and would always begin on a Sunday. All the remaining months would have just 30 days.
In such a setup, every date would land on the same day of the week every year. If your birthday fell on a Tuesday, it would always fall on a Tuesday. Independence Day would always fall on a Wednesday; Christmas Day would always be a Monday; and Thanksgiving would finally have a fixed date of November 23, since the fourth Thursday in November on the World Calendar would always land there.
Triskaidekaphobes, those who are superstitious of the number 13, likely would not be fans of the new setup. It would mean four Friday the 13ths every year. (Currently, the maximum number of Friday the 13ths in any given year is three.)
But Wait, This Is a 364-Day Calendar. What About Day 365 and Leap Years?
December 31 would be recognized as “Worldsday,” a World Holiday. It would come between Saturday the 30th and Sunday, January 1 of the new year. As for leap years, the extra day would not be tacked onto February. It would be inserted at the end of June. June 31 would become a second World Holiday, observed every four years like the Olympics.
In the January 17, 2016 issue of Parade magazine, Marilyn vos Savant answered a reader who asked whether there was a “less clunky” system than the calendar we use now.
Marilyn alluded to the Symmetry454 calendar, a perennial solar calendar that conserves the traditional seven-day week, has symmetrical equal quarters, and starts every month on Monday. All holidays, birthdays, and anniversaries would be permanently fixed. All ordinal day and week numbers within the year would also be permanently fixed. Friday the 13th never occurs under this calendar.
“But there’s a teensy drawback,” Marilyn notes. “Every five or six years, you would have to add a week at the end of December!”
Leap Year List, Past and Present

results.title: Leap year - Wikipedia
results.content:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Calendar year with a day (or month) added
A leap year (also known as an intercalary year or bissextile year[a]) is a calendar year that contains an additional day (or, in the case of a lunisolar calendar, a month) compared to a common year. The 366th day (or 13th month) is added to keep the calendar year synchronised with the astronomical year or seasonal year. Since astronomical events and seasons do not repeat in a whole number of days, calendars that have a constant number of days each year will unavoidably drift over time with respect to the seasons. By inserting an additional day—a leap day—or an additional month—a leap month—into some years but not others, the drift between a civilisation's dating system and the physical properties of the Solar System can be avoided.
An astronomical year lasts slightly less than 3651⁄4 days. The historic Julian calendar has three common years of 365 days followed by a leap year of 366 days, by extending February to 29 days rather than the common 28. The Gregorian calendar, the world's most widely used civil calendar, makes a further adjustment for the small error in the Julian algorithm; this extra leap day occurs in each year that is a multiple of 4, except for years evenly divisible by 100 but not by 400. Thus 1600, 2000 and 2400 are leap years, but 1700, 1800, 1900, 2100, 2200, and 2300 are not. In the Solar Hijri and Bahá'í calendars, a leap day is added whenever needed to ensure that the following year begins on the March equinox.
A lunar year of 12 lunar months is about 11 days shorter than an astronomical year. Lunisolar calendars, such as are traditional in most of Asia, each has its own rule to decide when to add a leap (lunar) month, so as to keep its calendar year from drifting through the seasons. Pure lunar calendars, such as the lunar Hijri calendar used in most of Islam, do not employ any such arrangement and accept the seasonal drift.
The term leap year probably comes from the fact that a fixed date in the Gregorian calendar normally advances one day of the week from one year to the next, but the day of the week in the 12 months following the leap day (from 1 March through 28 February of the following year) will advance two days due to the extra day, thus leaping over one day in the week. For example, since 1 March was a Friday in 2024, a Saturday in 2025, and a Sunday in 2026, and will be a Monday in 2027, the date will then "leap" over Tuesday to fall on a Wednesday in 2028.
The length of a day is also occasionally corrected by inserting a leap second into Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) because of variations in Earth's rotation period. Unlike leap days, leap seconds are not introduced on a regular schedule because variations in the length of the day are not entirely predictable.
On 1 January 45 BC, by edict, Julius Caesar reformed the historic Roman calendar to make it a consistent solar calendar (rather than one which was neither strictly lunar nor strictly solar), thus removing the need for frequent intercalary months. His rule for leap years was a simple one: add a leap day every 4 years. This algorithm is close to reality: a Julian year lasts 365.25 days, a mean tropical year about 365.2422 days, a difference of only ≈ 11⁠1/4⁠ min. Consequently, even this Julian calendar drifts out of 'true' by about 3 days every 400 years. The Julian calendar continued in use unaltered for about 1600 years until the Catholic Church became concerned about the widening divergence between the March equinox and 21 March, as explained at Gregorian calendar, below.
Prior to Caesar's creation of what would be the Julian calendar, February was already the shortest month of the year for Romans. In the Roman calendar (after the reform of Numa Pompilius that added January and February), all months except February had an odd number of days – 29 or 31. This was because of a Roman superstition that even numbers were unlucky. When Caesar changed the calendar to follow the solar year closely, he made all months have 30 or 31 days, leaving February unchanged except in leap years.
In the Gregorian calendar, the standard calendar in most of the world, almost every fourth year is a leap year. Each leap year, the month of February has 29 days instead of 28. Adding one extra day in the calendar every four years compensates for the fact that a period of 365 days is shorter than a tropical year by almost six hours. However, this correction is excessive and the Gregorian reform modified the Julian calendar's scheme of leap years as follows:
Every year that is exactly divisible by four is a leap year, except for years that are exactly divisible by 100, but these centurial years are leap years if they are exactly divisible by 400. For example, the years 1700, 1800, and 1900 are not leap years, but the years 1600 and 2000 are.
Whereas the Julian calendar year incorrectly summarised Earth's tropical year as 365.25 days, the Gregorian calendar makes these exceptions to follow a calendar year of 365.2425 days. This more closely resembles a mean tropical year of 365.2422 days. Over a period of four centuries, the accumulated error of adding a leap day every four years amounts to about three extra days. The Gregorian calendar therefore omits three leap days every 400 years, which is the length of its leap cycle. This is done by omitting 29 February in the three century years (multiples of 100) that are not multiples of 400. By this rule, an entire leap cycle is 400 years, which totals 146,097 days, and the average number of days per year is 365 + 1⁄4 − 1⁄100 + 1⁄400 = 365 + 97⁄400 = 365.2425. This rule could be applied to years before the Gregorian reform to create a proleptic Gregorian calendar, though the result would not match any historical records.
This graph shows the variations in date and time of the June Solstice.
The Gregorian calendar was designed to keep the March equinox on or close to 21 March, so that the date of Easter (celebrated on the Sunday after the ecclesiastical full moon that falls on or after 21 March) remains close to the March equinox. The "Accuracy" section of the "Gregorian calendar" article discusses how well the Gregorian calendar achieves this objective, and how well it approximates the tropical year.
Leap day in the Julian and Gregorian calendars
"Leap day" redirects here. For other uses, see Leap Day.
The intercalary day that usually occurs every four years is called leap day and is created by adding an extra day to February. This day is added to the calendar in leap years as a corrective measure because the Earth does not orbit the Sun in precisely 365 days. Since about the 15th century, this extra day has been 29 February, but when the Julian calendar was introduced, the leap day was handled differently in two respects. First, leap day fell within February and not at the end: 24 February was doubled to create, strangely to modern eyes, two days both dated 24 February. Second, the leap day was simply not counted so that a leap year still had 365 days.
The earliest Roman calendar was a lunisolar one, but it was abandoned about 450 BC by the decemviri, who implemented the Roman Republican calendar, used until 46 BC. The Republic's calendar consisted of 12 months, for a total of 355 days. In addition, a 27-day intercalary month, the Mensis Intercalaris, was sometimes inserted into February, at the first or second day after the Terminalia a. d. VII Kal. Mar. (23 February), to resynchronise calendar with the solar year. The remaining days of Februarius were discarded. This intercalary month, named Intercalaris or Mercedonius, contained 27 days. The religious festivals that were normally celebrated in the last five days of February were moved to the last five days of Intercalaris. The days of the months were counted down (inclusively) to the next named day, so 24 February was ante diem sextum Kalendas Martias ["the sixth day before the calends of March"] often abbreviated a. d. VI Kal. Mart. The Romans counted days inclusively in their calendars, so this was the fifth day before 1 March when counted in the modern exclusive manner (i.e., not including both the starting and ending day). Because only 22 or 23 days were effectively added, not a full lunation, the calends and ides of the Roman Republican calendar were no longer associated with the new moon and full moon.
In Caesar's revised calendar, there was just one intercalary day – nowadays called the leap day – to be inserted every fourth year, and this too was done after 23 February. To create the intercalary day, the existing ante diem sextum Kalendas Martias (sixth day (inclusive: i.e., what we would call the fifth day before) before the Kalends (first day) of March, i.e., what we would call 24 February) was doubled, producing ante diem bis sextum Kalendas Martias [a second sixth day before the Kalends. This bis sextum ("twice sixth") was rendered in later languages as "bissextile": the "bissextile day" is the leap day, and a "bissextile year" is a year which includes a leap day. This second instance of the sixth day before the Kalends of March was inserted in calendars between the "normal" fifth and sixth days. By legal fiction, the Romans treated both the first "sixth day" and the additional "sixth day" before the Kalends of March as one day. Thus a child born on either of those days in a leap year would have its first birthday on the following sixth day before the Kalends of March. In a leap year in the original Julian calendar, there were indeed two days both numbered 24 February. This practice continued for another fifteen to seventeen centuries, even after most countries had adopted the Gregorian calendar.[citation needed]
For legal purposes, the two days of the bis sextum were considered to be a single day, with the second sixth being intercalated; but in common practice by the year 238, when Censorinus wrote, the intercalary day was followed by the last five days of February, a. d. VI, V, IV, III, and pridie Kal. Mart. (the days numbered 24, 25, 26, 27, and 28 from the beginning of February in a common year), so that the intercalated day was the first of the doubled pair. Thus the intercalated day was effectively inserted between the 23rd and 24th days of February. All later writers, including Macrobius about 430, Bede in 725, and other medieval computists (calculators of Easter), continued to state that the bissextum (bissextile day) occurred before the last five days of February.[citation needed]
In England, the Church and civil society continued the Roman practice whereby the leap day was simply not counted, so that a leap year was only reckoned as 365 days. Henry III's 1236 Statute De Anno et Die Bissextili[b] instructed magistrates to treat the leap day and the day before as one day. The practical application of the rule is obscure. It was regarded as in force in the time of the famous lawyer Sir Edward Coke (1552–1634) because he cites it in his Institutes of the Lawes of England. However, Coke merely quotes the Act with a short translation and does not give practical examples.
... and by (b) the statute de anno bissextili, it is provided, quod computentur dies ille excrescens et dies proxime præcedens pro unico dii, so as in computation that day excrescent is not accounted.
Replacement (by 29 February) of the awkward practice of having two days with the same date appears to have evolved by custom and practice; the etymological origin of the term "bissextile" seems to have been lost. In England in the fifteenth century, "29 February" appears increasingly often in legal documents – although the records of the proceedings of the House of Commons of England continued to use the old system until the middle of the sixteenth century. It was not until the passage of the Calendar (New Style) Act 1750 that 29 February was formally recognised in British law.[c]
In the liturgical calendar of the Christian churches, the placement of the leap day is significant because of the date of the feast of Saint Matthias, which is defined as the sixth day before 1 March (counting inclusively). The Church of England's Book of Common Prayer was still using the "two days with the same date" system in its 1542 edition; it first included a calendar which used entirely consecutive day counting from 1662 and showed leap day as falling on 29 February. In the 1680s, the Church of England declared 25 February to be the feast of St Matthias. Until 1970, the Roman Catholic Church always celebrated the feast of Saint Matthias on a. d. VI Kal. Mart., so if the days were numbered from the beginning of the month, it was named 24 February in common years, but the presence of the bissextum in a bissextile year immediately before a. d. VI Kal. Mart. shifted the latter day to 25 February in leap years, with the Vigil of St. Matthias shifting from 23 February to the leap day of 24 February. This shift did not take place in pre-Reformation Norway and Iceland; Pope Alexander III ruled that either practice was lawful. Other feasts normally falling on 25–28 February in common years are also shifted to the following day in a leap year (although they would be on the same day according to the Roman notation). The practice is still observed by those who use the older calendars.[citation needed]

results.title: Leap Years – When is the Next Leap Year?
results.content:
Leap Years – When is the Next Leap Year?
A leap year adds one extra day to the calendar: February 29. That extra day keeps the calendar in sync with Earth’s orbit around the sun. Below, we break down what a leap year is, how the rule works, and what it means in the United States for holidays, payroll and Leap Day birthdays!
A leap year has 366 days instead of 365. It adds February 29 to keep the calendar aligned with Earth’s actual orbit around the sun.
When is the next leap year?
The next leap year is 2028, and Leap Day will fall on Tuesday, February 29. 572 days left until leap day.
Is Leap Day considered a US federal holiday?
No. February 29 is not a federal holiday in the United States, so government offices, schools, banks, and financial markets generally follow their normal weekday schedules.
How is a legal birthday determined for someone born on Leap Day?
In the United States, the answer depends on the state or agency. Many jurisdictions use March 1 in non-leap years, while some, including California in certain contexts, use February 28.
Year — February 29 — Detail / Countdown
2000 — Tuesday — 26 years ago
2004 — Sunday — 22 years ago
2008 — Friday — 18 years ago
2012 — Wednesday — 14 years ago
2016 — Monday — 10 years ago
2020 — Saturday — 6 years ago
2024 — Thursday — 2 years ago
2028 — Tuesday — In 1 y, 11 m, 6 d
2032 — Sunday — In 6 years
2036 — Friday — In 10 years
2040 — Wednesday — In 14 years
2044 — Monday — In 18 years
2048 — Saturday — In 22 years
2052 — Thursday — In 26 years
2056 — Tuesday — In 30 years
2060 — Sunday — In 34 years
2064 — Friday — In 38 years
2068 — Wednesday — In 42 years
2072 — Monday — In 46 years
2076 — Saturday — In 50 years
2080 — Thursday — In 54 years
2084 — Tuesday — In 58 years
2088 — Sunday — In 62 years
2092 — Friday — In 66 years
2096 — Wednesday — In 70 years
What Is a Leap Year and Why Is It Necessary?
A leap year has 366 days instead of the usual 365. The extra day is added to February, giving the calendar a February 29.
We need that extra day because Earth does not orbit the sun in exactly 365 days. A solar year is about 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes, and 56 seconds long. Those extra hours add up. Without periodic correction, the calendar would slowly drift away from the seasons.
Leap Day is the correction. By adding an extra day at regular intervals, the Gregorian calendar stays much closer to the actual seasonal year. Without that adjustment, the mismatch would grow over time, and the calendar would gradually fall out of step with the natural year.
When Is the Next Leap Year?
The next leap year is 2028, and Leap Day will fall on Tuesday, February 29.
You can print our PDF table showing every leap year from 2000 to 2104.
How Does the Leap Year Math and the 400 Year Rule Work?
A common shortcut says leap years happen every four years. That is mostly true, but not completely. The full rule is more precise.
A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4. But if it is divisible by 100, it is not a leap year unless it is also divisible by 400.
That is why the Gregorian calendar works better over long periods than a simple “every four years” rule.
The Sidereal Year vs. The Calendar Year
A calendar year has 365 days, but Earth’s orbit takes slightly longer. That small difference adds up over time, which is why we add February 29.
Years divisible by 100 are not leap years.
Years divisible by 400 are leap years.
Years divisible by 4 are leap years.
Why the Year 2100 Will Not Be a Leap Year: The year 2100 will not be a leap year because it is divisible by 100 but not by 400.
Is Leap Day a Federal Holiday in the United States?
No. February 29 is not a federal holiday in the United States.
That means most normal weekday operations continue as usual. Federal employees do not automatically receive the day off, and nonessential government offices generally remain open.
For most people, Leap Day works like an ordinary weekday unless it happens to fall under a separate local closure or schedule change.
How Does a Leap Year Affect Salaried Payroll and HR Compliance?
Leap years can create payroll issues, especially for employers that pay weekly or biweekly. The extra day can create an extra pay period, forcing employers to decide whether to keep paychecks the same or spread annual salary across more checks.
The 53 Week Payroll Anomaly
In a typical year, one weekday appears 53 times. In a leap year, two weekdays do, which increases the chance of an extra payday. That can mean 53 weekly pay periods instead of 52, or 27 biweekly pay periods instead of 26. The issue usually affects weekly and biweekly payroll more than semimonthly schedules.
Employers generally have two options:
Keep each paycheck the same, which may increase total annual pay.
Recalculate each paycheck across the higher number of pay periods.
What they cannot do is skip the extra paycheck.
FLSA Minimum Salary Thresholds and Withholding Risks
Recalculating pay across 53 weekly or 27 biweekly pay periods can create compliance problems if an exempt employee’s weekly pay drops below the required FLSA minimum salary threshold. That can raise FLSA wage-and-hour issues and, in some cases, jeopardize exempt status.
The extra pay period can also affect withholding and reporting for federal, state, local, Social Security, and Medicare taxes. For HR and payroll teams, this is a planning issue that should be reviewed before the first affected paycheck.
What Are the US Legal Rules for Leapling Birthdays and Age Limits?
People born on February 29 are often called leaplings or leapers. Their birthdays create a real legal question in non-leap years: when do age-based rights take effect if February 29 does not exist that year?
In the United States, there is no single nationwide answer. The rule depends on the jurisdiction and the agency involved.
State-by-State Differences: February 28 vs. March 1
Many US legal interpretations treat March 1 as the operative birthday in non-leap years, meaning a person legally reaches a new age only after February 28 has passed. California can treat February 28 differently, allowing some rights and deadlines to attach a day earlier. States with specific statutes, including Maine (§1406-A. – 4) and Nevada (NAC 483.043 – 4), may follow their own rules based on the wording of state law.
That difference can affect driver’s licenses, voting eligibility, military enlistment, alcohol purchases, and other age based rights.
Social Security and Federal Benefit Timelines
Federal benefits do not always follow the same logic as state age laws. For Social Security, the missing date usually matters less because benefit timing is generally based on the month and year of birth, not a day-by-day legal birthday analysis.
So while Leap Day birthdays can affect state level age thresholds, they usually do not create the same issue for federal retirement benefit timing.
What Are the Most Common Leap Year Traditions and Superstitions?
Leap years are not only about astronomy and calendars. They also come with long-running traditions, folklore, and a surprising number of superstitions.
Some of those traditions are celebrated openly. Others are treated as bad luck.
Anthony, Texas: The Leap Year Capital of the World
Anthony, on the Texas–New Mexico border, is widely known as the Leap Year Capital of the World. Since 1988, it has hosted Leap Year celebrations for people born on February 29.
The Tradition of Women Proposing Marriage
One of the best-known Leap Day traditions says women may propose marriage on February 29. The custom is usually linked to Irish folklore involving St. Brigid of Kildare and St. Patrick.
Global Superstitions Regarding Leap Year Luck
Leap years are seen as lucky in some places and unlucky in others. Greek folklore has long linked leap-year marriages to bad luck, and some Scottish traditions have treated Leap Day births negatively.
How Does a Leap Year Differ from a Leap Second?
A leap year and a leap second solve different timekeeping problems.
A leap year adds a full day to the calendar to help keep the year aligned with Earth’s orbit around the sun.
A leap second adds or subtracts a single second to keep highly precise time standards aligned with Earth’s rotation, which is not perfectly uniform.
Leap Year — Leap Second
Adds one day. — Adds or subtracts one second.
Happens on a predictable calendar rule. — Happens irregularly when needed.
Keeps the calendar aligned with Earth’s orbit. — Keeps precise time aligned with Earth’s rotation.
Mainly affects calendars and date based planning. — Mainly affects technical systems, computing and precision timekeeping.

results.title: Roman superstition and modern calendars. Why February has 28 days
results.content:
Is 2026 a leap year? What to know about the calendar's shortest month
Sarah Moore Lansing State Journal
Why are there leap years? Is 2026 a leap year?
Here's why we have leap years, adding an extra day in February. Does 2026 qualify?
February's unique length on the modern-day calendar is derived from the Romans' alterations and superstitions while they were in power in Italy centuries ago.
February has 28 days most years — including in 2026 — but it will have 29 once again in 2028 during the next leap year. The last leap year was in 2024.
The four-year fluctuation keeps calendars we use on a daily basis in line with winter, spring, summer and fall. The Romans played a role in the necessity by creating a lunar-based calendar, then changing it several times. Throughout their tinkering, and that of later calendar makers February was the only month with fewer than 30 days.
Here's more on February's unique number of days, and why leap year is important:
Why is February a short month?
The Roman calendar attributed to the Roman King Numa Pompilius (715-673 BC) set February up to be an odd month a long time ago. The Romans divided the year into 10 months, from March to December, of either 29 or 31 days based on lunar cycles and the superstition that even numbers were unlucky, according to BBC Sky at Night Magazine.
The rest of the year after December was unnamed: It was considered unimportant since people didn't plant or harvest crops in the winter, according to the magazine.
Pompilius eventually added January and February to make a full year, however, February was left with 28 days.
"When Numa Pompilius took reign [of Rome], he decided to make the calendar more accurate by lining it up with the year’s 12 lunar cycles," according to the Children's Museum of Indianapolis. "The new 355-day year needed two additional months to make up for the lost time. So he added January and February to the end of the calendar."
During Julius Caesar's rule (46-44 BC), the calendar no longer matched the actual seasons because the lunar cycle and calendar months didn't match. To realign the calendar, Caesar adopted a 365-day calendar based on the sun's orientation and added 10 days, including a leap day in February every four years, calendar.com said.
Finally, the calendar we all know was adopted by Catholic Pope Gregory XIII in 1582, after skipping 10 days in October to "catch up," it has changed little since then.
What is the purpose of a leap year?
Leap years account for the inaccurate measure of time on the 365-day calendar. Technically it takes 365.242190 days for the Earth to orbit the sun, according to the National Air and Space Museum.
By adding a day to February every four years, approximately, the calendar years adjust to the "sidereal year," the actual time it takes for the Earth to orbit the sun.
If that's not confusing enough, every so often we skip a leap year so we don't add too much time to the calendar.
No, 2026 is not a leap year. Leap years occur every four years so the next is 2028, then 2032 and 2036.
February birthdays: What happens if yours lands on the leap day?
If you have a birthday on Feb. 29, the leap day, you can celebrate your birthday on March 1, or maybe Feb. 28. Unfortunately, you don't avoid aging.

results.title: Is 2026 a leap year? Everything you need to know.
results.content:
Does February 2026 have a 'bonus' day in store? See upcoming Leap Days
What is a leap year? Here's the science behind the extra day.
Why do we have leap years? The reason behind that extra day on Feb. 29 is more complicated than you think.
With the end of February right around the corner, you might be wondering if the shortest month of the calendar year will be extended by a day, one leap day, if you will.
Leap days and corresponding leap years, which "helps keep us in sync with the seasons," only comes around every so often, National Geographic Kids reports.
Since the calendar oddity typically happen every four years (although there are some exceptions), the next leap is skipping 2026 altogether and will happen in 2028. Our last Leap Days were in 2024 and 2020.
People, especially "Leaplings," have celebrated the "bonus" day in different ways over the years, with businesses offering special deals in commemoration and others finally celebrating their Feb. 29 birthday.
Here's everything you need to know.
2026 is not a leap. The last leap year (and corresponding leap day) occurred Feb. 29, 2024. It was a Thursday.
Leap Day is essentially a "bonus" day that is added to the calendar every four years. During a leap year, Leap Day falls on Feb. 29, adding one day to the shortest month of the calendar year.
According to NatGeo Kids, leap days are important because they help our calendar match up with the same seasons every year.
Why is Leap Day every four years?
We earthlings have Leap Days, and years, because of our planet's orbit.
It takes the Earth 365.242190 days, not 365 days as we've been led to believe by human-made calendars, to complete a full revolution around the sun.
While .2422 of a day doesn't seem like it would make too much of a difference, "ignoring that fraction means eventually our seasons won’t fall in the same months every year," NatGeo Kids reports.
The change would gradually impact other aspects of life, like the growing and harvest of crops, which has the potential to affect food supplies.
When added, four .2422 days roughly equal one full day, which is why Feb. 29 is added to the calendar of most years divisible by four.
The next Leap Day (and year) won't be for a while: 2028, 2032 and 2036.
Though rare, sometimes we'll skip leap years to make up for decimals of time. Since years divisible by 100 but not 400 are skipped, the next leap year we'll skip is quite a ways away, in 2100.
Contributing: Emily Vetter and Olivia Munson, USA TODAY

One year has the length of 365 days, 5 hours, 48 minutes and 45 seconds. These are 365.2421875 days. This is hard to calculate with, so for practical reasons a normal year has been given 365 days and a leap year 366 days. In leap years, February 29th is added as leap day, which doesn't exist in a normal year. A leap year is every 4 years, but not every 100 years, then again every 400 years. So the year 1900 wasn't a leap year, but 2000 was.
This year 2026 isn't a leap year. The last leap year was 2024, the next will be 2028.
The fact that the length of a year is not divisible by the length of a day without a remainder was already known in ancient times. To solve this problem, Julius Caesar set the leap day on February 29th in 45 BCE when he introduced the Julian calendar. This improved the calendar enormously and pushed the problem of days not matching exactly several centuries into the future. But a quarter of a day (six hours), which is delayed every four years by the leap day, is a little more than 5 hours, 48 ​​minutes and 45 seconds. And at some point the error became apparent in that the days of the year were at a different point in the seasonal cycle. The Julian calendar was one day too slow every 128 years. In 1582, Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar, and in that year the 4th was followed by the 15th of October, making up ten days. It took a good 200 years for it to become accepted worldwide. The solution that every 100 years is not a leap year, but every 400 years is, represented the true length of the day in a year fairly well, but not completely accurately. The Gregorian calendar is one day too slow every 3231 years, so in the distant future a day will have to be skipped in the calendar. This will probably be a leap day that then will not occur.

results.content:
Fun facts about leap years
This Thursday, Feb. 29, is leap day. You might know that a leap year generally occurs every four years, but you might not know the reason for this rule or that there is an exception to it.
Keep reading for fun facts about leap years.
Why do we have leap years?
The 365 days of a regular calendar year is actually an approximation of the time it takes the Earth to orbit the sun. According to NASA, it takes approximately 365.25 days for Earth to complete a full orbit around the Sun. Since it’s hard to add a quarter of a day into a calendar every year, we round down to 365 days per year, and extra hours from each regular year get added up into a leap day that occurs every four years. In other words, leap years keep the calendar lined up with the Earth’s actual orbit.
Which years are leap years?
Leap years generally occur on any year that is divisible by four. For example, 2024 is divisible by four, so it is a leap year. However, 2025, 2026 and 2027 are not divisible by four, so they are regular years. This rule was created when the Julian calendar came into use in Ancient Rome.
However, when the western world switched to the Gregorian calendar in the late 16th Century, an exception to the four year rule was introduced. Because it takes slightly less than 365.25 days for Earth to orbit the Sun, having leap years every four years with no breaks would actually push the calendar out of sync with the seasons after a couple of centuries. To keep the calendar accurate, years divisible by 100 but not by 400 are not leap years. That means that 2100, 2200 and 2300 will have 365 days, but 2400 will have 366 days.
Spend the leap day wisely, Bruins — the next one won’t come for another four years!

Is this year a leap year? When is the next leap year?
Manahil Ahmad NorthJersey.com
How leaplings celebrate their birthday on leap years
A leap year has an extra day in February causing those born on Feb. 29 to only get a birthday every four years
Leap years occur on a regular cycle to keep the calendar aligned with Earth’s orbit around the sun, adding an extra day to the month of February every four years.
A leap year contains 366 days instead of the usual 365. The adjustment accounts for the fact that Earth takes about 365¼ days to complete one orbit around the sun. Without the extra day added periodically, the calendar would drift by roughly six hours each year, eventually causing the seasons to fall out of sync with calendar dates.
When is the next leap year?
The next leap year will take place in 2028, when an additional day Feb. 29 will be added to the calendar. The date will fall on Tuesday, Feb. 29, 2028. Because leap years occur every four years, 2026 will not be a leap year. Following 2028, the next leap years will be 2032 and 2036.
The calculation follows specific rules. A year is a leap year if it is divisible by four. However, century years, those ending in “00” must also be divisible by 400 to qualify. For example, 2000 was a leap year because it was divisible by 400, while 1900 was not. The year 2100 will also not qualify as a leap year under that rule.
The system, embedded in the Gregorian calendar, has been used for centuries to maintain long-term alignment between civil time and astronomical reality.

Leap years, and why 2026 isn’t one
This video shows why we have leap years. And it shows what happens if we don’t..
Why 2026 isn’t a leap year
The last leap year was 2024. So 2028 will be our next leap year, a 366-day-long year, with an extra day added to our calendar (February 29). We’ll call that extra day a leap day. It’ll help synchronize our human-created calendars with Earth’s orbit around the sun and with the passing of the seasons. Why do we need the extra day? Blame Earth’s orbit. Our planet takes approximately 365.25 days to orbit the sun once. It’s that .25 that creates the need for a leap year every four years.
During non-leap years, aka common years – like 2026 – the calendar doesn’t take into account the extra quarter of a day required by Earth to complete a single orbit. In essence, the calendar year, which is a human artifact, is faster than the solar year, the 365 days 5 hours 48 minutes 46 seconds that our planet requires to orbit the sun once.
Over time and without correction, the calendar year would drift away from the solar year. And the drift would add up quickly. For example, without correction the calendar year would be off by about one day after four years. It’d be off by about 25 days after 100 years. You can see that, if even more time were to pass without the leap year as a calendar correction, eventually February would be a summer month in the Northern Hemisphere.
Leap years and the Gregorian calendar
Leap days were first added to the Julian Calendar in 46 BCE by Julius Caesar at the advice of Sosigenes, an Alexandrian astronomer.
In 1582, Pope Gregory XIII revised the Julian calendar by creating the Gregorian calendar with the assistance of Christopher Clavius, a German mathematician and astronomer. The Gregorian calendar stated that leap days should not be added in years ending in “00” unless that year is also divisible by 400. This additional correction was added to stabilize the calendar over a period of thousands of years and was necessary because solar years are actually slightly less than 365.25 days. In fact, a solar year occurs over a period of 365.2422 days.
So, according to the rules set forth in the Gregorian calendar, leap years have occurred or will occur during the following years:

Notice that 2000 was a leap year because it is divisible by 400, but that 1900 was not a leap year.
Since 1582, the Gregorian calendar has been gradually adopted as a “civil” international standard for many countries around the world.
In medieval Ireland and Scotland, women were allowed to propose marriage to men on February 29 of any leap year. A man who rejected the proposal owed a fine to the woman.
Children born on Leap Day have a true birthday every four years. They generally will celebrate their birth on February 28 or March 1.
Some cultures consider a leap year unlucky – for people or animals – all year long.
Bottom line: 2026 isn’t a leap year. But 2028 will be. Why do we have leap years?
